identity.author: John Davenant
identity.work: Two Dissertations (De praedestinatione through Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2)
identity.edition: Dissertationes duae (Cambridge: Roger Daniel, 1650). Partial through Cap. X Propos. 2 Aug. witnesses. Further Cap. X remains.

scope.locus: De praedestinatione Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III + Propos. 2 open.
scope.next_locus: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2 cont. (Epist. 107; Prosper; Milevis/Orange on non-universal saving grace; then Propos. 3 mere good pleasure).

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1 close toward III: Hague Colloquy grants no more than Pelagius — all stall refusing the grace that by infused faith and charity makes the good will
english: Last hear the Hague Colloquists: they grant infusion of divine grace as to intellect and affections, but deny such infusion in the will, as free by nature to will good or evil. In all this I see nothing credited to divine grace that Pelagius himself would not have granted. Mind’s illumination, kindling of affections, and by these a push on the will and power to will the good—Pelagius fetches from grace; but that the will becomes good by its own act without any infused gift, and is quickened by its own act, even Pelagius scarcely said so clearly. See how far Pelagius, with Pelagians and Semipelagians, and Arminius with his followers, go in owning divine grace—and see them all stuck at the same mark, refusing the most efficacious grace that, faith and charity inspired, makes the good will, and admitting only the grace that makes the will able to become good by its own doing, if it wills to be good by doing well.
sections.latin: Ultimo in loco Collocutores Hagienses audiantur, qui infusionem Divinae gratiae agnoscunt quidem quoad intellectum et affectus, in voluntate autem negant istiusmodi infusionem locum habere, ut quae natura sua libera sit ad volendum bonum vel malum. In hisce omnibus nihil video gratiae Divinae tribui quod Pelagius ipse non concessisset. Illam mentis illuminationem et affectuum accensionem, et hisce mediantibus propulsionem voluntatis, et potentiam ad bonum volendum, a gratia arcessit Pelagius; Verum, actione sua (absque omni dono infuso) bonam fieri, et vivificari voluntatem sua propria actione, vix tam clare asseveravit ipse Pelagius. Videtis jam quousque in agnitione gratiae Divinae processit Pelagius, cum Pelagianis et Semipelagianis, Arminius etiam cum sectatoribus suis: videtis etiam eos omnes ad eandem metam haerere, neque velle admittere illam efficacissimam gratiam, qua inspirata fide et charitate voluntatem bonam facit, sed illam solummodo, qua potens redditur ut sua actione bona evadat, si ipsa velit esse bona, agendo bene.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III: the Grace of Christ the Fathers pressed is what Pelagius and Arminius explode as free will’s coercive — Bishop of Salisbury De vera grat. Christi p.60
english: III. What remains in this first proposition: what grace Augustine with the other Orthodox contended Pelagius must acknowledge—and which they named by excellence the Grace of Christ. We affirm it was none other than the grace Pelagius and Arminius explode as free will’s coercive. We cannot paint it in fitter words than the Reverend Bishop of Salisbury (De vera gratia Christi, p. 60): This is the true grace Christian faith owns and believes, by which God gives his laws into our minds and writes them on our hearts; by which, when he requires our will, he himself makes us will; when he bids convert, he makes us convert at once; when he demands faith, by his gift he makes us believe.
sections.latin: III. Veniamus ad illud quod in hac prima propositione nostra restat explicandum; Qualis nimirum fuerit ea gratia, quam Augustinus una cum reliquis Orthodoxis a Pelagio agnosci contendebant, quamque per excellentiam Gratiam Christi indigitabant. Affirmamus autem, non aliam fuisse quam hanc quam Pelagius et Arminius quasi liberi arbitrii coactivum exploserunt. Non possumus autem eam aptioribus vocabulis depingere, quam depicta est a Reverendo Episcopo Sarisburiensi, De vera grat. Christi, pag. 60. Haec, inquit ille, est vera gratia, quam Christiana fides agnoscit et credit, qua Deus dat leges suas in mentes nostras, et in cordibus nostris inscribit eas; qua ubi requirit voluntatem nostram, facit ipse ut velimus; ubi converti jubet, facit simul ut convertamur; ubi fidem postulat, facit dono suo ut credamus.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III: Augustine — true grace is inspiration of love; he makes us walk and do; adjutorium whereby something is done; not only to be able but to will
english: A few from Augustine (Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum 4.5): he describes true grace as the inspiration of love, that we may do what is known with holy love—that is proper grace. And 4.6: We walk, we keep, we do—but he makes us walk, keep, do. This is God’s grace making us good; this his mercy going before us. He calls this grace of Christ a help whereby something is done. From it, he says, there is in us not only power to do what we will, but also to will what we can (De correptione et gratia 11–12).
sections.latin: Ex Augustino paucula delibemus: Contra 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 4. cap. 5. gratiam veram sic describit, Inspiratio dilectionis, ut cognita sancto amore faciamus, propria gratia est. Et cap. 6. Nos ambulamus, nos observamus, nos facimus, sed ille facit ut ambulemus, ut observemus, ut faciamus. Haec est gratia Dei bonos faciens nos, haec misericordia ejus praeveniens nos. Hanc gratiam Christi vocat adjutorium quo aliquid fit. Dicit ab hac gratia esse in nobis non solum posse quod volumus, verum etiam velle quod possumus, De corr. et grat. cap. 11. et 12.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III: grace that only warns and persuades, leaving the will under free will’s dice, is law not proper grace — Aug. De grat. Christi 13–14
english: But of the grace that only warns and persuades, and leaves the will under free will’s uncertain dice, Augustine holds it looks to law rather than to grace properly so called (De gratia Christi contra Pelagium 13): Who knows what ought to be done and does not, has not yet learned from God according to grace, but according to law. And at the start of 14: Who has not come is not yet rightly said to have learned—he heard and learned that he ought to come, but will not do what he learned. That mode of teaching is not rightly called the way God teaches by grace.
sections.latin: De illa autem gratia quae monet et suadet tantum, sed ipsam Voluntatem quasi sub alea incerta liberi sui arbitrii relinquit, sentit Augustinus, ad legem potius eam spectare quam ad gratiam proprie dictam: Qui novit quid fieri debeat, et non facit, nondum a Deo didicit secundum gratiam, sed secundum legem, De gratia Christi, contra Pelag. cap. 13. Et initio cap. 14. Qui non venit, nondum ille recte dicitur didicisse: audivit quidem et didicit oportere veniendum, sed facere non vult quod didicit. Prorsus non recte dicitur de isto docendi modo, quo per gratiam docet Deus.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III: not Augustine alone — Milevis can. 4, African exiles, Orange can. 4 preach creating/vivifying grace that works both to will and to do
english: Someone will say this was Augustine’s private view, pulled in by absolute predestination. No: it was common to all the Orthodox, as the anti-Pelagian councils show. Milevis canon 4: By Christ’s grace it is granted us that what we know ought to be done, we also love and can do. A little later: Both are God’s gift—to know what we ought to do, and to love so that we do. The synodical letter of the African bishops exiled in Sardinia is the same: God commands a man to will, but the Lord works in the man also to will; he commands to do, but works also to do. In quickening men God waits for no start of the human will; he quickens by making the good will itself. Orange canon 4 is clear: If anyone contends God waits for our will so we may be purged from sin, and does not confess that even our willing to be purged is wrought in us by the Spirit’s infusion and working, he resists the Holy Spirit speaking through Solomon, The will is prepared by the Lord, and the Apostle, It is God who works in us both to will and to finish according to his good will.
sections.latin: Sed dixerit aliquis, Haec fuit singularis Augustini sententia, in quam absolutae praedestinationis opinio eum pertraxit. Imo fuit omnium Orthodoxorum communis, ut ex Conciliis contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos celebratis constat. Ex Milevitano, canone 4, Per gratiam Christi nobis praestatur, ut quod faciendum cognoverimus, etiam facere diligamus atque valeamus. Paulo post, Utrumque donum Dei est, et scire quid facere debeamus, et diligere ut faciamus. Ex Epistola Synodica Episcoporum Africanorum in Sardinia exsulum idem patet: Jubet Deus homini ut velit, sed Dominus in homine operatur et velle: jubet ut faciat, sed operatur et facere. Deus in vivificandis hominibus nullum initium humanae voluntatis exspectat, sed ipsam voluntatem bonam faciendo vivificat. Demum ex Concilio Arausicano idem liquet; canone 4, Si quis, ut a peccato purgemur, voluntatem nostram Deum exspectare contendit, non autem ut etiam purgari velimus per Sancti Spiritus infusionem et operationem in nos fieri confitetur, resistit ipsi Spiritui Sancto per Solomonem dicenti, Praeparatur voluntas a Domino, et Apostolo salubriter praedicanti, Deus est qui operatur in nobis et velle et perficere pro bona sua voluntate.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1 close: illuminating/exciting grace is not the Grace of Christ Orthodoxy pressed — that grace creates the good will; received grace is not wage of a non-resisting will
english: Why so much on the grace of Christ? So it is clear from Orthodox common consent: the illuminating, warning, exciting grace that—if Arminians are believed—fails no mortal, yet in many lacks a saving effect, is not the Grace of Christ to whose acknowledgment the Orthodox meant to drive Pelagius. That grace creates the good will, sanctifies the man, and at last infallibly produces salvation’s effect. The Master of the Sentences knew this sense (lib. 2, dist. 26, lit. D): Grace preventing and preparing the will is faith with love. So Aquinas (1a2ae q.111 a.3) when he assigned it five effects: that the soul be healed, will the good, work the good it wills, persevere in the good, and reach glory. Let this stand fixed: received Grace of Christ is not the wage of a non-resisting will; the non-resisting will is the effect of that grace given and received. Enough for the first proposition.
sections.latin: Quorsum haec tam multa de gratia Christi? Ut intelligatur, Ex communi consensu Orthodoxorum, gratiam illam illuminatricem, monitricem, et excitatricem, quae nulli mortalium deest (si credimus Arminianis) quaeque effectu salutifero in plurimis caret, non esse eam gratiam Christi, ad cujus agnitionem Pelagium adigere Orthodoxi voluerunt; sed eam quae voluntatem bonam creat, hominem sanctificat, ac denique effectum salutis infallibiliter producit. Hunc esse sensum hujus vocabuli non latuit Magistrum Sententiarum, lib. 2. dist. 26. lit. D. Gratia, inquit, voluntatem praeveniens et praeparans, est fides cum dilectione. Hanc etiam gratiam intellexit Aquinas, 1. 2. qu. 111. art. 3. quando quinque effecta ei assignavit, nempe, ut anima sanetur, ut bonum velit, ut bonum quod vult operetur, ut in bono perseveret, ut ad gloriam perveniat. Maneat ergo hoc fixum et stabilitum, Gratiam Christi receptam non esse mercedem voluntatis non-resistentis, sed non-resistentem voluntatem esse effectum hujus gratiae donatae ac receptae. Atque haec ad primae propositionis explicationem abunde sufficiant.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2 open: this Grace of Christ was prepared from eternity and given in time to some, to others neither — event proves; ‘given to all but not all receive’ fails
english: I pass to the second: This grace of Christ was prepared from eternity and given in time to some; to others neither prepared nor given. Few words are needed—the thing speaks. From the event we see that efficacious grace is not given to all; and that for those never given it, it was never prepared from God’s eternal good pleasure, is beyond doubt. Who is so witless as to say faith and charity are given and infused to all, or a good will created in all, or perseverance and glory granted to all? Nor does the dodge hold: God gives these to all, but all do not receive. Whoever God has given a good will, faith, charity, perseverance is presumed to have received them all. Gifts are said to be given not to those who lack them, but to those who enjoy them.
sections.latin: Transeo ad secundam: Ea fuit hujusmodi; Haec gratia Christi quibusdam praeparata fuit ab aeterno et donata in tempore, quibusdam nec praeparata nec donata. Hic multis verbis haud opus est, nam res ipsa loquitur. Videmus siquidem ex eventu non dari omnibus praedictam gratiam efficacem; et quibus nunquam fuit data, iis ex aeterno Dei beneplacito nunquam fuisse praeparatam, extra omnem dubitationis aleam ponendum est. Quis autem tam excors ut dicat fidem et charitatem omnibus donari et infundi? aut bonam voluntatem in omnibus creari? aut perseverantiam et gloriam omnibus concedi? Neque hic locum habere potest illa exceptio, Deus haec dat omnibus; sed omnes non accipiunt. Nam cuicunque data est a Deo bona voluntas, fides, charitas, perseverantia, ille haec omnia accepisse praesumitur. Donata enim dicuntur, non illis qui talibus donis carent, sed qui iisdem gaudent.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2: Augustine restricts vivifying grace to the predestined and purpose-called — De grat. Christi 12–13; De praedest. sanct. 9; faith a gift to some not all
english: What was the Orthodox view? From Augustine we have almost endless witnesses. Excellent is De gratia Christi contra Pelagium et Caelestium 12–13: This grace whereby strength is perfected in weakness leads the predestined and those called according to purpose to the highest perfection and glorification. God pours this grace in more deeply and inwardly with unspeakable sweetness—not only through those who plant and water outwardly, but through himself, who secretly gives the increase—so that he not only shows the truth but imparts charity. So he restricts this grace to the predestined and purpose-called, and shows it is efficacious not from the event alone but from the giver’s purpose and the nature of the grace given. That such grace is not given to all is clearer than noon. No less clear is De praedestinatione sanctorum 8: Faith begun and perfected is God’s gift; and that this gift is given to some and not to others, let no one doubt who will not contradict the plainest Scripture.
sections.latin: Sed videamus quae fuerit hac de re Orthodoxorum sententia. Ex Augustino habemus infinita paene testimonia. Praeclarum est illud, De gratia Christi contra Pelag. et Caelestium, cap. 12. et 13. Haec gratia qua virtus in infirmitate perficitur, praedestinatos et secundum propositum vocatos ad summam perfectionem glorificationisque perducit. Hanc gratiam Deus altius et interius cum ineffabili suavitate infundit, non solum per eos qui plantant et rigant extrinsecus, sed etiam per seipsum, qui incrementum suum ministrat occultus, ita ut non ostendat tantummodo veritatem, verum etiam impertiat charitatem. Hisce verbis hanc gratiam ad praedestinatos et secundum propositum vocatos restringit, atque simul ostendit, non esse efficacem ex eventu solummodo, sed ex proposito dantis, et ex ipsa datae gratiae natura. Talem gratiam omnibus non dari, meridiana luce clarius est. Non minus illustre est illud alterum testimonium, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 8. Fides inchoata et perfecta donum Dei est: et hoc donum quibusdam dari, quibusdam non dari, omnino non dubitet qui non vult manifestissimis sacris literis repugnare.
